Posted April 24, 2001
(MarijuanaNews note: From the " Just when we thought that they couldn’t get any stupider " files…

There is often an odd synchronicity about the workings of marijuana prohibition, so I sometimes come across stories from different corners of the world that reflect the same ideological processes.

The two items below are an excellent example of this phenomenon, but -- more substantively -- they demonstrate that the irrationality of marijuana prohibition makes it a threat to everyone, not just marijuana users.

Moreover, these stories point out certain natural allies in our struggle for freedom. A major topic at the recent NORML conference was the need to build coalitions. We cannot fight this battle alone, and should not have to. The health food industry has more experience resisting the therapeutic police state than perhaps any other, and they have been very successful for the most part. We need to reach out to them and make clear that our struggle is really their struggle, as well.

At the

Inasmuch as hemp production is legal in Canada, and the same store sells Canadian hemp seed oil as a food, I was amazed. However, the special Canadian label refers the perplexed to a page on Dr. Bronner’s web site, which is the first item below.

It seems that Health Canada, which could more honestly be called " Control Canada, " is concerned that diluting hemp seed oil with other ingredients might somehow increase the minuscule THC levels. This would be a very neat trick, violating all of the laws of physics. Less may equal more in some aesthetics, but not in the physical world.

However, this is not the first display of reefer madness from Health Canada.

The second item below comes from another hemp producing country, Australia, where production has also just begun recently. That story clearly demonstrates that marijuana prohibition is a threat to everyone’s health -- and indifferent to the suffering of the sick and dying. We see evidence of that every day in the battle for medical marijuana, but it goes far beyond that.

Again, the point here is that the irrationality of marijuana prohibition makes it a threat to everyone.)

Hemp oil is an excellent choice to make into soap because of its high Essential Fatty Acid (EFA) content. Adding hemp to our soap has improved the moisturizing and afterfeel dramatically. The lather now is smoother, milder and creamier.

In late July, Canadian Customs stopped a shipment of our soaps at the border. The soaps could not enter because of their hemp oil content. Not only is all of the hemp oil we use certified and compliant with Canadian regulations, with the THC content at less than 10 parts per million*, but we actually use oil purchased in Canada in the first place! Health Canada is not interested in the fact that we can document that the hemp oil that goes into the soap is certified Canadian compliant; they only want to see the finished product tested.

Here is Health Canada's second irony: There is no official protocol for such a test presently available for a water-based soap like ours (only one for hemp oil itself). We are not presently able to ship our liquid and bar soaps into Canada because of this strange " Catch-22 " bureaucratic reasoning.

We make our soap from coconut oil, olive oil and hemp oil. We add essential oils to make each variety different. Each finished product obviously contains less hemp oil than the 100% pure hemp oil we have imported from Canada. Thus, our soap has that much less THC, substantially less than the regulated level of 10 parts per million.

Health Canada's Industrial Hemp Office knows and understands these points very clearly. When we asked Canadian companies how they deal with the problems we face, they replied that two years ago, when the industry was just starting in Canada, this exact issue had to be dealt with. At that time, the Industrial Hemp Office recognized that official analysis for hemp oil is not appropriate for testing finished formulations. For Canadian manufacturers, Health Canada accepts as proof that if the original hemp oil is in compliance, then the finished product, with that hemp oil as just one of the ingredients, will be in compliance. Canadian manufacturers are not required to test finished formulations.

In other words, Health Canada wants us to subject our product to a test that does not exist; yet Canadian companies are not required to test. Health Canada states that we must develop at our own cost a way to test our product. They will then take an undetermined length of time to review and approve the test (we were warned it takes a long time). But even if they were to approve, it would add substantially to the cost of every batch of soap we make for shipment to Canada, making it cost prohibitive for us to ship. We believe that they are being unfair and unreasonable.

There is no conceivable possible way that more THC would appear in our soap than is contained in the diluted, certified hemp oil itself. Health Canada fully recognizes this fact, and does not hold Canadian manufacturers to this unreasonable standard. Thus, they are in effect blockading American imports of hemp formulations, which forces us to either withdraw our soaps from the Canadian marketplace or reformulate the soaps for sale into Canada without hemp oil.

Our soaps are still terrific without the hemp oil, but the lather and afterfeel are not nearly as smooth without the hemp oil and its essential fatty acids. Until this situation is resolved, we will realign our production and logistics to specially produce de-hemped liquid soap for sale in Canada. Unfortunately, it is not feasible for us to do this with the bar soaps, so these will not be available until our soaps are free to be as great as they can be with the hemp oil.

Canadian customers please help us!

Please write a letter to your local MP on our behalf (no stamp required: MP's name, House of Commons, Ottowa, Ontario), and copy letters to the Minister of Health (currently Allan Rock, no stamp required: Minister of Health, House of Commons, Ottowa, Ontario) as well as to Senator Lorna Milne who is helping us out (no stamp required: Senator Lorna Milne, Senate of Canada, Ottowa, Ontario).

Thank you for your patronage, and any efforts you make to help us.

All-One! The Bronner Family

*THC is the therapeutically active component of medical marijuana, a controversial cousin of industrial hemp. Industrial hemp is bred for its oilseed and fiber for industrial products and is itself too low in THC to produce any psychoactive effect. Hemp oil from the seed of industrial hemp contains levels of THC two to five thousand times less than medically active doses in medical marijuana.

CUSTOMS SWOOP JOLTS MS SUFFERER

A BRITISH tourist with multiple sclerosis is outraged that Australian Customs confiscated hemp oil recommended by his doctor.

Mark Eden, 36, came to WA on March 26 to visit his 2 1/2,*-year-old son.

Hemp seed oil is sold over the counter in Britain but Mr Eden said he knew it might be difficult to take overseas.

" I contacted Customs in Perth through e-mails and on the phone, " he said. " They told me as long as I had a doctor's letter stating why I took it, it would not be a problem. "

But when he declared at Perth Airport that he was carrying four 250ml bottles of the substance, Customs officers took him aside and he was questioned by Australian Federal Police.

" I felt like I was being treated like a criminal when I take the oil for a medical condition, " he said.

Mr Eden said he took the oil to help treat a chronic skin irritation caused by his condition. It did not give him a high.

Customs service spokesman Leon Bedington said hemp oil was a prohibited import. A Customs officer had made it clear to Mr Eden that a doctor's prescription or a permit would be needed to allow it into Australia.

" The passenger satisfied neither condition, " Mr Bedington said.

The AFP had sent the oil for analysis. Federal police would consult Customs once they had the results.

Australian Drug Law Reform Foundation WA president Jason Meotti, who is related to Mr Eden, said the incident highlighted the inadequacy of Australian laws when a product available for medical purposes overseas was confiscated.
